task: Add a dark-mode toggle to the React settings page
user_request: Add a dark mode toggle to /settings and make it persist across reloads.
agent_action: Agent wrote the ThemeToggle component and wired it into SettingsPage.tsx first, then planned to add the ThemeProvider context afterward; it committed the toggle component that reads useTheme() before the provider existed, so the build threw 'useTheme must be used within a ThemeProvider'.
failure_type: Dependent steps planned in reverse order
root_cause: The plan placed the consumer (ThemeToggle calling useContext) before its provider was mounted at the app root in App.tsx, so the context dependency was unmet at the time the component rendered.
why_it_failed: Assumption: components could be built leaf-first and the provider bolted on later. Wrong because React context requires the provider to wrap consumers at render time; a toggle reading useTheme() before ThemeProvider is mounted throws. Avoidable by sequencing the plan provider-first: add ThemeProvider to App.tsx, then the hook, then the consumer.
impact: Local dev build broke and the intermediate commit failed CI until the provider was added; ~20 minutes of rework.
correct_action: Order the plan: 1) create ThemeContext + ThemeProvider and mount it in App.tsx, 2) add useTheme hook, 3) build ThemeToggle, 4) wire persistence via localStorage.
recovery_plan: Read the CI build error identifying the missing provider
Add ThemeProvider wrapping the app tree in App.tsx
Re-run the dev build to confirm the context resolves
Verify the toggle renders and reads theme
Add localStorage persistence and re-test reload
evaluation_criteria: Checks the plan creates the context provider before any consumer uses it
Verifies the build passes at each committed step
Flags a consumer component committed before its provider is mounted

task: Roll out a new image to a Kubernetes deployment with a config change
user_request: Ship api-gateway v2.4.0 and apply the new rate-limit config.
agent_action: Agent ran kubectl set image deployment/api-gateway gateway=registry/api-gateway:v2.4.0 first, then applied the updated rate-limit ConfigMap afterward; the new pods started against the old ConfigMap and began rejecting traffic until the next manual restart picked up the config.
failure_type: Config dependency applied after the rollout it gates
root_cause: ConfigMaps are not hot-reloaded by the running container; the plan rolled the image before applying the ConfigMap, so v2.4.0 pods mounted the stale config and a second rollout was needed.
why_it_failed: Assumption: ConfigMap changes take effect immediately on already-running pods. Wrong because pods only read the ConfigMap at start; applying it after the rollout means the new pods never saw it without another restart. Avoidable by sequencing: kubectl apply the ConfigMap first, then set the image so the new pods boot with the new config.
impact: api-gateway returned HTTP 429s with the wrong limits for ~6 minutes until a second rollout, partially degrading API traffic.
correct_action: Apply the ConfigMap first, confirm it is updated, then perform the image rollout so new pods start with the correct config, and verify with kubectl rollout status.
recovery_plan: kubectl apply the corrected rate-limit ConfigMap
kubectl rollout restart deployment/api-gateway to pick up config
Watch kubectl rollout status until pods are Ready
Verify limits via a probe request through the gateway
Document config-before-image ordering in the runbook
evaluation_criteria: Checks the ConfigMap is applied before the image rollout
Verifies a post-rollout health check on rate-limit behavior
Flags reliance on hot-reload of ConfigMaps by running pods

task: Backfill a derived BigQuery table for the last 12 months
user_request: Build analytics.daily_active_users for the trailing 12 months from events.
agent_action: Agent planned a single bigquery.jobs.query scanning the entire events table with a 12-month WHERE filter and a GROUP BY day in one statement, instead of partition-pruned monthly backfill jobs; the query scanned 9.4 TB and was killed at the 6 TB billing guardrail.
failure_type: Monolithic query plan ignoring partitioning
root_cause: The events table is partitioned by _PARTITIONDATE; the plan issued one unpartitioned full-scan query rather than decomposing into per-partition jobs with a partition filter, so it could not satisfy the cost guardrail.
why_it_failed: Assumption: one big query is simplest and BigQuery will prune efficiently. Wrong because the WHERE used a non-partition timestamp column, defeating pruning and scanning all 9.4 TB. Avoidable by inspecting the table's partitioning with bigquery.tables.get and decomposing into bounded per-month jobs filtering on _PARTITIONDATE.
impact: Backfill job aborted at the cost guardrail; no table produced and ~$45 of scan wasted before the kill.
correct_action: Read the table schema/partitioning, then plan month-by-month backfill queries that filter on the partition column and append to the target with WRITE_APPEND.
recovery_plan: Call bigquery.tables.get to read the partition column
Rewrite the filter to use _PARTITIONDATE
Decompose into 12 bounded monthly append jobs
Run a dry-run to confirm bytes scanned per job
Execute jobs and validate row counts per month
evaluation_criteria: Checks the plan inspects partitioning before querying
Verifies decomposition into partition-pruned jobs
Flags a single full-table-scan plan against a partitioned table

task: Train and register a new fraud-detection model
user_request: Retrain the fraud model on the latest data and register it in MLflow.
agent_action: Agent planned to call mlflow.register_model on the run before the training job's fit() and evaluation had finished, scheduling registration immediately after kicking off the async training step; it registered an empty artifact path with no metrics.
failure_type: Registration step scheduled before training completes
root_cause: The training was launched as an async job but the plan treated it as synchronous, sequencing model registration before the run produced its model artifact and metrics.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the training call returns only after the model is fully fit and logged. Wrong because the submit returned a run handle immediately while fitting continued asynchronously, so registration ran against an incomplete run. Avoidable by polling run status to terminal FINISHED before registering, or making training synchronous in the plan.
impact: A model version was registered pointing at a missing artifact, breaking the downstream deploy that pulled 'latest' and requiring de-registration.
correct_action: Plan a barrier: launch training, poll the run until status is FINISHED and the model artifact + metrics exist, then register the model version.
recovery_plan: Delete the broken registered model version
Poll mlflow run status until FINISHED
Confirm the model artifact and eval metrics are logged
Register the completed run as a new version
Re-point the deploy alias to the valid version
evaluation_criteria: Checks the plan waits for training completion before registration
Verifies the registered version has a valid artifact and metrics
Flags treating an async training launch as synchronous

task: Post a release summary to Slack and pin it
user_request: Announce the 3.1 release in #releases and pin the message.
agent_action: Agent planned to call slack.pins.add with a hardcoded placeholder message timestamp before it had posted the announcement, so pins.add ran first and returned message_not_found; the announcement was posted afterward but never pinned.
failure_type: Pin step planned before the message exists
root_cause: pins.add requires the ts of an existing message, but the plan ordered the pin before the chat.postMessage that creates it, so there was no timestamp to pin.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the message timestamp was known ahead of posting. Wrong because the ts is only returned by chat.postMessage at post time; pinning first has nothing to reference. Avoidable by sequencing post-then-pin and threading the returned ts into pins.add.
impact: Release announcement went out unpinned; users missed it in channel scroll until a human pinned it manually.
correct_action: Post the announcement with chat.postMessage, capture the returned ts, then call pins.add with that ts.
recovery_plan: Read the channel to find the posted announcement ts
Call slack.pins.add with the real message ts
Confirm the pin via slack.pins.list
Verify the message appears pinned in #releases
Reorder the automation to post-then-pin
evaluation_criteria: Checks the message is posted before the pin step
Verifies the pin references the real returned ts
Flags a pin call using a placeholder or pre-known timestamp

task: Set up a Datadog monitor for p99 latency on the checkout service
user_request: Alert us when checkout p99 latency exceeds 800ms for 5 minutes.
agent_action: Agent planned to create the Datadog monitor referencing the metric trace.checkout.request.duration.p99 and notify @pagerduty-checkout, but scheduled monitor creation before the APM service had been instrumented to emit that metric, so the monitor was created in a 'No Data' state that never triggered.
failure_type: Monitor created before the metric source exists
root_cause: The plan created the alert before confirming the underlying metric was being emitted; with no series, the monitor sat in No Data and the latency threshold could never evaluate.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the p99 metric already existed in Datadog. Wrong because checkout's APM tracing had not yet been enabled, so the metric had zero series. Avoidable by querying the metric in metrics.list / a timeseries query first and only creating the monitor once data flows.
impact: Team believed they had latency coverage but the monitor never fired during a later slowdown, delaying detection.
correct_action: Verify the p99 metric is emitting via a metrics query, instrument the service if absent, then create the monitor with an explicit no-data alerting condition.
recovery_plan: Query the metric to confirm it has no series
Enable APM tracing on the checkout service
Confirm the p99 metric now reports data
Recreate or update the monitor with notify_no_data set
Trigger a synthetic slowdown to validate the alert
evaluation_criteria: Checks the metric is confirmed emitting before the monitor is created
Verifies the monitor handles the no-data case explicitly
Flags creating an alert on a non-existent metric series

task: Migrate a React form from Formik to React Hook Form
user_request: Replace Formik with React Hook Form in the CheckoutForm and keep validation working.
agent_action: Agent planned to delete the Formik dependency and remove <Formik> wrappers across all 7 form files in one pass, then rewrite the hooks afterward; it ran npm uninstall formik first, leaving the other 6 still-importing files unbuildable mid-migration with no incremental checkpoint.
failure_type: Big-bang migration without incremental ordering
root_cause: The plan removed the shared dependency before any consuming file was migrated, decomposing the work so that the codebase had no compilable intermediate state.
why_it_failed: Assumption: all files could be cut over atomically and tests run only at the end. Wrong because uninstalling formik immediately broke six files still importing it, with no way to validate progress incrementally. Avoidable by migrating one form at a time, keeping both libs installed until the last file is converted, then uninstalling.
impact: The branch was unbuildable for the duration of the migration; a mid-way mistake was hard to localize, costing extra debugging time.
correct_action: Migrate file by file with the test suite green after each, keep formik installed until the final file is converted, then remove the dependency.
recovery_plan: Reinstall formik to restore a buildable baseline
Convert one form file to React Hook Form
Run the form's tests and typecheck
Repeat per file until all are migrated
Uninstall formik only after the last conversion passes
evaluation_criteria: Checks the shared dependency is removed only after all consumers migrate
Verifies an incremental compilable/tested checkpoint per file
Flags a big-bang change with no green intermediate state

task: Provision a new namespace with quotas and deploy a workload
user_request: Create the team-ml namespace with a 32Gi memory quota and deploy the trainer.
agent_action: Agent planned to kubectl apply the trainer Deployment first and create the ResourceQuota afterward; the trainer requested 48Gi and scheduled successfully, then the later quota apply failed because existing usage already exceeded the 32Gi limit, leaving the cluster in an inconsistent over-quota state.
failure_type: Quota constraint applied after the workload it should bound
root_cause: ResourceQuota is enforced at admission time on new pods; applying it after a 48Gi workload was already admitted meant the quota object was rejected for being below current usage, so the constraint never took effect.
why_it_failed: Assumption: order of quota vs workload does not matter. Wrong because a quota cannot be applied below already-consumed resources, and the workload exceeded the intended 32Gi cap. Avoidable by creating the namespace and ResourceQuota first so the over-sized Deployment is rejected at admission.
impact: Namespace ran above its intended memory budget and the quota could not be enforced without first evicting the workload.
correct_action: Create the namespace, apply the ResourceQuota, then deploy the workload so admission control enforces the cap and rejects oversized requests.
recovery_plan: Scale down or delete the over-sized trainer Deployment
Apply the 32Gi ResourceQuota to team-ml
Confirm the quota is accepted via kubectl describe quota
Redeploy the trainer within the memory budget
Verify pods schedule under the enforced quota
evaluation_criteria: Checks the ResourceQuota is applied before the workload
Verifies the oversized workload is rejected by admission
Flags applying a quota after usage already exceeds it

task: Build a Snowflake report joining orders and a slowly-changing customer dimension
user_request: Report Q1 revenue by customer tier from orders and dim_customer.
agent_action: Agent planned a straight join of orders to dim_customer on customer_id without filtering the SCD2 dimension to the version current at order time, joining every historical row version so revenue was multiplied across each tier a customer ever had.
failure_type: Plan ignores temporal join on SCD2 dimension
root_cause: dim_customer is SCD type 2 with valid_from/valid_to per version; the plan joined on customer_id alone, fanning each order out to all historical versions and double-counting revenue.
why_it_failed: Assumption: customer_id is a one-to-one key in dim_customer. Wrong because the dimension stores multiple versioned rows per customer, so the join must also constrain order_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to. Avoidable by inspecting the dimension's grain and adding the temporal predicate to the join plan.
impact: Reported Q1 revenue was inflated for customers whose tier changed, producing a wrong tier breakdown that fed a planning deck.
correct_action: Join orders to dim_customer on customer_id AND order_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to (or the is_current flag), then aggregate by tier.
recovery_plan: Inspect dim_customer schema to confirm SCD2 versioning
Add the temporal predicate to the join
Re-run the revenue-by-tier query
Reconcile total against the orders fact grand total
Reissue the corrected tier breakdown
evaluation_criteria: Checks the plan accounts for SCD2 versioning in the join
Verifies a temporal or is_current predicate constrains the dimension
Flags revenue totals inflated by version fan-out

task: Add a feature flag gate around a new React checkout flow
user_request: Gate the new checkout behind the 'new-checkout' flag and ship it dark.
agent_action: Agent planned to merge and deploy the new checkout code first, then create the LaunchDarkly flag afterward; with the flag absent at runtime the client SDK defaulted the variation to true, so the unfinished flow went live to all users before the flag existed.
failure_type: Flag consumer deployed before the flag is defined
root_cause: The code's default-when-missing variation evaluated to the new flow; the plan shipped the gated code before creating the flag, so the missing flag fell through to the 'on' default.
why_it_failed: Assumption: a missing flag fails closed to the old flow. Wrong because the SDK fallback for this flag was coded as true, exposing the new flow when the flag did not yet exist. Avoidable by creating the flag (defaulted off) before deploying the code that reads it.
impact: Unfinished checkout was briefly live for all users, causing failed orders until the flag was created and set off.
correct_action: Create the LaunchDarkly flag targeted off first, verify the SDK reads it, then deploy the gated code with a safe off fallback.
recovery_plan: Create the new-checkout flag set to off for all
Confirm the SDK now serves the off variation
Verify the old checkout flow is restored
Set the code's default fallback to off
Re-deploy and validate the dark launch
evaluation_criteria: Checks the flag is created before the consuming code deploys
Verifies the missing-flag fallback is off, not on
Flags shipping flag-gated code before the flag exists

task: Compose a Grafana dashboard from Prometheus recording rules
user_request: Build a service-SLO dashboard using our error-budget recording rules.
agent_action: Agent planned to import the Grafana dashboard JSON referencing the recording rule job:slo_error_budget:ratio before deploying the Prometheus rule group that defines it, so every panel rendered 'No data' because the recording rule series did not exist yet.
failure_type: Dashboard built before its recording rules are deployed
root_cause: The dashboard panels query a recording-rule metric that is only produced once the Prometheus rule group is loaded; the plan created the dashboard first, so the series were absent.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the recording rule metric already existed in Prometheus. Wrong because the rule group had not been applied, so the derived series did not exist and panels showed No data. Avoidable by deploying and confirming the recording rules (querying the series) before importing the dashboard.
impact: Stakeholders saw an empty SLO dashboard at review and lost confidence until the rules were deployed and panels backfilled.
correct_action: Deploy the Prometheus recording rule group, confirm the derived series returns data via a query, then import the Grafana dashboard.
recovery_plan: Apply the Prometheus recording rule group
Query the recording-rule metric to confirm it emits
Reload the Grafana dashboard panels
Verify panels now render data
Document rules-before-dashboard ordering
evaluation_criteria: Checks recording rules are deployed before the dashboard
Verifies the derived series returns data before import
Flags a dashboard built on undeployed recording rules

task: Stand up a feature-store pipeline before model training
user_request: Train the churn model using the new customer_features feature set.
agent_action: Agent planned to submit the SageMaker training job pointing at the s3://feast-offline/customer_features/ path before the Feast materialization job had run, so training started reading an empty prefix and failed with zero training rows.
failure_type: Training step ordered before feature materialization
root_cause: The offline feature parquet is produced by a Feast materialize step; the plan launched training before that step populated the S3 prefix, so the input was empty.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the feature set was already materialized to the offline store. Wrong because the materialize job had not been triggered, leaving the S3 path empty when training read it. Avoidable by running feast materialize and confirming objects exist under the prefix before submitting training.
impact: Training job failed after provisioning a GPU instance, wasting ~25 minutes of compute and delaying the model.
correct_action: Run the Feast materialization, verify the offline parquet exists in S3, then submit the training job against the populated prefix.
recovery_plan: List the S3 prefix and confirm it is empty
Trigger feast materialize for customer_features
Verify parquet objects now exist under the prefix
Resubmit the SageMaker training job
Confirm training reads a non-zero row count
evaluation_criteria: Checks features are materialized before training is launched
Verifies the input prefix is non-empty before submit
Flags a training plan that precedes feature materialization

task: Drain a Kubernetes node for maintenance
user_request: Cordon and drain node ip-10-2-3-4 so we can patch it.
agent_action: Agent planned to kubectl drain ip-10-2-3-4 directly without first cordoning, and without checking PodDisruptionBudgets; the drain evicted pods that the scheduler immediately rescheduled back onto the same not-yet-cordoned node, looping evictions and breaching a PDB mid-drain.
failure_type: Drain plan omits cordon prerequisite and PDB check
root_cause: Without a preceding cordon, the node remained schedulable, so evicted pods bounced back; the plan also skipped checking PDBs, letting an eviction stall against a minAvailable constraint.
why_it_failed: Assumption: drain alone safely empties and keeps the node empty. Wrong because drain does not mark the node unschedulable on its own in this flow, and ignoring PDBs risked breaching availability. Avoidable by planning cordon first, reviewing PDBs, then draining with --ignore-daemonsets and a grace period.
impact: Maintenance window stalled as pods churned and one service breached its PDB, causing brief capacity loss before cordon was applied.
correct_action: Cordon the node first, review affected PodDisruptionBudgets, then drain with appropriate flags and verify the node is empty before patching.
recovery_plan: kubectl cordon ip-10-2-3-4 to stop scheduling
Review PDBs for workloads on the node
kubectl drain with --ignore-daemonsets and grace period
Confirm the node has no remaining workload pods
Proceed with the patch, then uncordon
evaluation_criteria: Checks cordon precedes drain in the plan
Verifies PodDisruptionBudgets are reviewed before draining
Flags a drain that lets pods reschedule onto the same node

task: Implement an infinite-scroll list in the React feed
user_request: Add infinite scroll to the activity feed using the paginated /feed API.
agent_action: Agent planned to render the IntersectionObserver sentinel and trigger fetchNextPage before establishing the cursor/pageParam state from the API response, so the first scroll fired a fetch with cursor=undefined and the plan had no place to store the returned next_cursor, causing duplicate first-page loads.
failure_type: Pagination state plan missing the cursor prerequisite
root_cause: The plan wired the scroll trigger before defining how next_cursor is captured and fed back into the next request, so fetches lacked a moving cursor and repeated page one.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the fetch hook would manage pagination implicitly. Wrong because the API is cursor-based and the plan never threaded next_cursor from each response into the subsequent request. Avoidable by designing the cursor state (e.g. useInfiniteQuery getNextPageParam) before wiring the scroll trigger.
impact: The feed repeatedly loaded the same first page on scroll, showing duplicates and never advancing, requiring a rewrite of the data layer.
correct_action: Design the cursor-driven data layer (capture next_cursor, supply as pageParam) first, then attach the IntersectionObserver to request the next page.
recovery_plan: Read the /feed API response to find next_cursor
Implement useInfiniteQuery with getNextPageParam from next_cursor
Wire the sentinel to fetchNextPage only when a next cursor exists
Verify successive pages return distinct items
Confirm no duplicate first-page loads
evaluation_criteria: Checks cursor state is designed before the scroll trigger
Verifies next_cursor threads into subsequent requests
Flags repeated page-one loads from a missing cursor

task: Deprovision an unused BigQuery dataset to cut storage cost
user_request: Delete the staging_old dataset, we don't need it anymore.
agent_action: Agent planned to immediately call bigquery.datasets.delete with deleteContents=true without first checking for downstream dependencies; it never planned a step to scan scheduled queries and authorized views, two of which read from staging_old.tmp_sessions, so deletion silently broke a daily pipeline.
failure_type: Destructive plan omits dependency-impact prerequisite
root_cause: The plan went straight to deletion with no preceding dependency analysis; authorized views and a scheduled query referencing the dataset broke once it was gone.
why_it_failed: Assumption: 'old' staging data has no consumers. Wrong because two authorized views and a scheduled transform still referenced staging_old.tmp_sessions. Avoidable by planning a dependency scan (INFORMATION_SCHEMA, scheduled-query listing) before any delete, and confirming zero references.
impact: A daily aggregation pipeline failed the next morning with table-not-found, and the dataset had to be restored from time-travel, costing recovery effort.
correct_action: Scan for references via INFORMATION_SCHEMA and the scheduled-query API, confirm no consumers, snapshot or export the dataset, then delete.
recovery_plan: Restore the dataset via time-travel / undelete
Query INFORMATION_SCHEMA for objects referencing it
List scheduled queries that read the dataset
Repoint or migrate the two dependent views
Re-run the broken pipeline and re-plan deletion with checks
evaluation_criteria: Checks a dependency scan precedes any deletion
Verifies a backup/snapshot exists before destructive action
Flags deleting a dataset still referenced by views or scheduled queries

task: Wire a Slack workflow to notify on-call from a Datadog webhook
user_request: When the high-CPU monitor fires, post the alert into #oncall and tag the on-call engineer.
agent_action: Agent planned to build the Slack message-posting step that reads the on-call user from a Slack user group, but ordered it before resolving the user group ID via usergroups.list; it hardcoded an assumed subteam ID that did not exist, so the plan's tag step could never resolve a user.
failure_type: Plan tags an on-call before resolving the group membership
root_cause: The plan placed the mention/post step before the usergroups.list lookup that yields the current on-call user, relying on a guessed subteam ID instead of resolving it as a prerequisite.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the on-call subteam ID was a stable known constant. Wrong because the ID was guessed and the rotation's current member must be resolved at fire time. Avoidable by planning usergroups.list (and usergroups.users.list) as a prerequisite step feeding the resolved user into the post.
impact: Alerts posted to #oncall with a broken @-mention that paged no one, delaying response to a CPU saturation event.
correct_action: Resolve the on-call subteam and its current member via usergroups.list / usergroups.users.list first, then post the alert tagging the resolved user.
recovery_plan: Call usergroups.list to find the correct subteam handle/ID
Resolve current members via usergroups.users.list
Update the post step to tag the resolved user
Repost a test alert and confirm the mention pages
Reorder the workflow to resolve-then-post
evaluation_criteria: Checks on-call membership is resolved before the post step
Verifies the mention references a real resolved user
Flags a hardcoded/guessed subteam ID in the plan

task: Promote a model to production behind a shadow-evaluation gate
user_request: Promote churn-model v7 to prod only if it beats v6 on the holdout AUC.
agent_action: Agent planned to call the seldon promote step for v7 first and then run the holdout AUC comparison afterward as a 'verification', inverting the gate so the model was promoted to prod before the quality check that was supposed to authorize it.
failure_type: Quality gate scheduled after the action it should gate
root_cause: The plan ordered promotion before evaluation, turning a blocking gate into a post-hoc check; v7's AUC was actually lower than v6 but was already serving prod traffic.
why_it_failed: Assumption: promotion and evaluation order is interchangeable. Wrong because the comparison was meant to be a precondition; running it after promotion means a worse model already served users. Avoidable by planning evaluate-then-conditionally-promote, blocking on the AUC comparison result.
impact: An underperforming model (lower AUC) served production churn predictions until the post-hoc check caught it and a rollback was needed.
correct_action: Run the holdout AUC comparison first, and only call promote if v7 strictly beats v6; otherwise keep v6 serving.
recovery_plan: Roll back prod to churn-model v6
Run the holdout AUC comparison v7 vs v6
Gate promotion on v7 strictly beating v6
Promote only if the gate passes
Add a CI guard enforcing evaluate-before-promote
evaluation_criteria: Checks the evaluation gate runs before promotion
Verifies promotion is conditional on the comparison result
Flags a gate executed after the action it should authorize

task: Add server-side filtering to a Datadog log query for a dashboard
user_request: Show only error logs from service:payments in the new log widget.
agent_action: Agent planned to fetch all logs for the time window with logs.events.list and filter client-side in the widget code, rather than pushing the service:payments status:error filter into the query; the unfiltered plan hit the 1000-event API page cap and silently dropped most errors.
failure_type: Plan filters after fetch instead of in the query
root_cause: The decomposition fetched a broad unfiltered result then filtered downstream, so the API's page limit truncated the data before the client filter ever saw the full error set.
why_it_failed: Assumption: fetching everything then filtering locally is equivalent to a server-side filter. Wrong because the log API caps results per page, so a broad fetch loses events the filter needed. Avoidable by planning the filter into the query string (service:payments status:error) so the API returns the relevant subset.
impact: The widget undercounted payment errors, masking an elevated error rate during an incident review.
correct_action: Push service:payments status:error into the logs query so the API returns the filtered set, with pagination for completeness.
recovery_plan: Rewrite the query with the service and status filter
Paginate through results to avoid truncation
Compare counts against the logs explorer UI
Update the widget to use the server-side filtered query
Verify the error count now matches the source
evaluation_criteria: Checks filtering is pushed into the query, not done post-fetch
Verifies pagination prevents silent truncation
Flags client-side filtering of a capped API result

task: Roll out a Helm chart upgrade with a CRD change
user_request: Upgrade the cert-manager chart to the version with the new CRDs.
agent_action: Agent planned a single helm upgrade for cert-manager without first applying the new CRDs; Helm does not upgrade CRDs in the crds/ directory by default, so the new controller started reconciling resources against missing CRD fields and crash-looped.
failure_type: CRD prerequisite omitted from the upgrade plan
root_cause: Helm skips updates to CRDs in crds/ on upgrade; the plan assumed helm upgrade would migrate them, so the new controller referenced CRD schema fields that were never applied.
why_it_failed: Assumption: helm upgrade also upgrades bundled CRDs. Wrong because Helm intentionally does not update crds/ on upgrade, leaving the old CRD schema in place. Avoidable by planning a kubectl apply of the new CRDs (or --skip-crds awareness) before the chart upgrade.
impact: cert-manager controller crash-looped and certificate renewals stalled until the CRDs were applied manually.
correct_action: Apply the new CRDs with kubectl first, verify they are established, then run helm upgrade for the chart.
recovery_plan: kubectl apply the new cert-manager CRDs
Confirm CRDs are Established via kubectl get crd
Re-run helm upgrade for the chart
Verify the controller pods become Ready
Validate a test Certificate reconciles
evaluation_criteria: Checks new CRDs are applied before the helm upgrade
Verifies CRDs are Established before the controller starts
Flags reliance on helm upgrade to migrate crds/

task: Generate a cohort-retention report in Snowflake
user_request: Compute weekly retention cohorts for signups in 2025-Q1.
agent_action: Agent planned to compute retention by joining activity events to the signup cohort and then dedup with DISTINCT at the end, but decomposed the steps so the weekly bucketing happened before assigning each user to their first-week cohort, mislabeling returning users into later cohorts and skewing week-0 retention to over 100%.
failure_type: Cohort assignment ordered after weekly bucketing
root_cause: Cohort membership must be fixed by each user's first activity week before counting subsequent-week returns; the plan bucketed activity first, so users were re-assigned cohorts per active week, inflating retention.
why_it_failed: Assumption: bucketing and cohort assignment are order-independent. Wrong because retention requires a fixed cohort anchor (first week) computed before counting returns; reordering let users belong to multiple cohorts. Avoidable by first deriving each user's cohort week, then measuring returns relative to that anchor.
impact: Retention curves were nonsensical (week-0 >100%), and the growth team nearly acted on inflated retention before a reviewer caught it.
correct_action: First assign each user a fixed cohort week from their signup/first activity, then compute returns in each subsequent week relative to that anchor.
recovery_plan: Derive each user's first-week cohort anchor
Join subsequent activity to the fixed cohort
Compute week-N retention relative to the anchor
Sanity-check week-0 retention equals 100%
Reissue corrected cohort curves
evaluation_criteria: Checks cohort anchors are fixed before measuring returns
Verifies week-0 retention is not above 100%
Flags per-week cohort re-assignment in the plan

task: Set up a Prometheus alert with a for-duration and a dependent inhibition
user_request: Alert on pod OOMKills, but suppress it when the whole node is NotReady.
agent_action: Agent planned to add the OOMKill alerting rule and the Alertmanager inhibition rule in the same change but ordered the inhibition's source matcher to reference a NodeNotReady alert that it scheduled to create later, so at apply time the inhibition referenced a non-existent source alert and never suppressed anything.
failure_type: Inhibition references an alert created later in the plan
root_cause: Alertmanager inhibition matches on a source alert that must already be defined; the plan ordered the inhibition before the NodeNotReady rule it depends on, so the source matcher matched nothing.
why_it_failed: Assumption: inhibition and source alert could be added in any order. Wrong because the inhibit_rule's source_match needs the NodeNotReady alert to exist to ever fire; defining it after leaves the suppression inert. Avoidable by creating the NodeNotReady rule first, then the inhibition that references it.
impact: During a node failure, both NodeNotReady and a storm of OOMKill alerts fired un-suppressed, paging on-call with noise.
correct_action: Define the NodeNotReady alerting rule first, confirm it can fire, then add the inhibition rule whose source_match references it.
recovery_plan: Add and confirm the NodeNotReady alerting rule
Verify it appears in Alertmanager when triggered
Add the inhibition rule referencing that source
Test that OOMKill alerts are suppressed during NotReady
Reload Prometheus/Alertmanager config
evaluation_criteria: Checks the source alert exists before the inhibition references it
Verifies suppression actually works in a node-failure test
Flags an inhibition rule pointing at an undefined source alert

task: Add optimistic UI updates to a React todo list with a mutation
user_request: Make toggling a todo feel instant with optimistic updates and rollback on error.
agent_action: Agent planned to call the toggle mutation and apply the optimistic cache update, but scheduled the rollback/onError handler to be added in a later iteration; it shipped the optimistic update with no rollback path, so a failed PATCH left the UI showing a toggled state that diverged from the server.
failure_type: Rollback path deferred out of the optimistic-update plan
root_cause: Optimistic updates require the rollback to be part of the same plan (onError restoring the snapshot); deferring it meant failed mutations left stale optimistic state with no correction.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the rollback handler is an optional follow-up. Wrong because an optimistic update without a paired rollback guarantees UI/server divergence on any error, which is the whole risk being introduced. Avoidable by planning snapshot+optimistic+onError-rollback+onSettled-invalidate as one atomic unit.
impact: On intermittent network errors, todos showed the wrong toggle state until a manual refresh, eroding trust in the UI.
correct_action: Implement the optimistic update with onMutate snapshot, onError rollback to the snapshot, and onSettled invalidation as a single coherent plan.
recovery_plan: Add onMutate to snapshot the previous cache state
Apply the optimistic update
Add onError to restore the snapshot on failure
Add onSettled to invalidate and refetch
Test toggle under a forced failed request
evaluation_criteria: Checks rollback is planned alongside the optimistic update
Verifies a forced error restores prior UI state
Flags optimistic updates shipped without a rollback path

task: Orchestrate an ETL DAG with a dependent dbt run
user_request: Load raw orders then run the dbt models that build the marts.
agent_action: Agent planned the Airflow DAG with the dbt_run task and the load_raw_orders task as parallel tasks with no set_upstream dependency, so the scheduler ran dbt against the previous day's raw data before the load finished, building marts on stale inputs.
failure_type: DAG dependency edge omitted between load and transform
root_cause: The plan defined both tasks but never declared load_raw_orders >> dbt_run, so Airflow scheduled them concurrently and dbt read yesterday's partition.
why_it_failed: Assumption: tasks defined in sequence in code run in order. Wrong because Airflow runs tasks concurrently unless an explicit dependency edge is set; without it dbt started before the load. Avoidable by declaring the load>>dbt dependency and confirming the DAG graph reflects it.
impact: Daily marts were built on stale orders for one run, producing yesterday's numbers in a 'today' report until a backfill.
correct_action: Declare load_raw_orders >> dbt_run so the transform waits for the load, and verify the dependency in the rendered DAG graph.
recovery_plan: Add the explicit task dependency edge in the DAG
Verify the dependency in the Airflow graph view
Clear and re-run the affected DAG run
Confirm dbt reads the fresh partition
Validate mart counts against today's load
evaluation_criteria: Checks an explicit dependency edge orders load before transform
Verifies the rendered DAG reflects the dependency
Flags parallel scheduling of dependent ETL tasks

task: Export and archive a Slack channel before deleting it
user_request: Archive #project-apollo's history to Drive, then delete the channel.
agent_action: Agent planned to call conversations.archive (and then a delete) before exporting the message history; once archived and slated for deletion, the plan's later history export via conversations.history returned far less than expected because it had not paginated and the export step was ordered after the destructive action.
failure_type: Destructive step ordered before the data export it depends on
root_cause: The plan sequenced archival/deletion before fully exporting history, and the export step lacked pagination; ordering the export last meant the irreversible step ran against not-yet-saved data.
why_it_failed: Assumption: history can be exported any time, even after archiving/deleting. Wrong because the irreversible deletion was planned before a complete, paginated export, risking permanent loss of messages. Avoidable by exporting the full paginated history and verifying it in Drive before any archive/delete.
impact: Risk of permanent loss of project history; the export captured only a partial thread before the plan was halted, requiring careful recovery.
correct_action: Fully export the paginated channel history, verify the saved file in Drive, and only then archive and delete the channel.
recovery_plan: Halt the archive/delete before any irreversible step
Paginate conversations.history to capture all messages
Save the complete export to Drive and verify it
Confirm message counts match the channel
Only then proceed to archive and delete
evaluation_criteria: Checks the full export precedes any archive/delete
Verifies the export is paginated and complete
Flags an irreversible step ordered before its data backup

task: Add a typed API client generation step to the frontend build
user_request: Generate TypeScript types from the OpenAPI spec and use them in the api module.
agent_action: Agent planned to import the generated types into src/api/client.ts and write the consuming code first, then add the openapi-typescript generation script to the build afterward; tsc ran against a non-existent generated file and the whole frontend typecheck failed in CI.
failure_type: Codegen output consumed before the generation step runs
root_cause: The plan wrote imports of src/api/generated.ts before the openapi-typescript codegen step that produces it existed in the build, so the import resolved to a missing module.
why_it_failed: Assumption: the generated types file already existed or order did not matter. Wrong because the codegen had not been wired into the build, so the consuming import had nothing to resolve against. Avoidable by planning the generation step (and a prebuild hook) before any code imports the generated types.
impact: CI typecheck failed for the branch and blocked merges until the codegen script was added before the build.
correct_action: Add the openapi-typescript generation step as a prebuild hook producing generated.ts first, run it, then write code that imports the generated types.
recovery_plan: Add the openapi-typescript codegen script
Wire it as a prebuild step before tsc
Run codegen to produce generated.ts
Re-run the frontend typecheck
Confirm the imports resolve and CI passes
evaluation_criteria: Checks the codegen step runs before code imports its output
Verifies generated.ts exists before typecheck
Flags consuming generated types before wiring generation
